name: Caffeine mesotherapy

card.summary: Injections of caffeine-containing solutions into the skin of fatty or cellulite-prone areas, used in clinics with the aim of reducing local fat and smoothing contours.
card.note: Mesotherapy is practitioner-administered and its regulation varies by country; skin infections have been reported after mesotherapy generally.

quick.overview:
Caffeine mesotherapy refers to mesotherapy, small injections just under the skin, using caffeine-containing preparations in areas where people want less fat or smoother skin, such as thighs, abdomen or under the chin. The idea behind it is that caffeine stimulates the breakdown of fat in the treated area.
Mesotherapy was developed in France and is practised in clinics and spas around the world. Wikipedia reports that mesotherapy in general has limited scientific backing and that the main FDA-approved injectable for fat is deoxycholic acid for the area beneath the chin; no caffeine-specific trials are cited.
quick.how: A practitioner delivers many tiny injections or uses a needle-free pressurised device across the target area, usually in repeated sessions, sometimes alongside other ingredients. This page does not describe formulations or technique.
quick.risks: Reports of mesotherapy in general include bruising, swelling, skin abscesses and a mycobacterial infection cluster in Australia, often linked to unhygienic practice. Some countries restrict it, and oversight in the US falls to state medical boards. Anyone considering it would discuss it with a licensed clinician.

lead: Caffeine mesotherapy is the use of caffeine-containing preparations in mesotherapy, a technique in which small amounts of pharmaceutical or other substances are injected into or just under the skin. Mesotherapy is also done with vitamins, plant extracts and hyaluronic acid, and a needle-free version uses a jet of air to deliver ingredients.[1]

In appearance terms, the aim is local fat reduction and smoother contours, for example on the thighs or abdomen. Proponents of mesotherapy say it targets fat cells; Wikipedia notes that there is no conclusive proof that any compound does so specifically, and the American Society for Dermatologic Surgery has said further study is needed.[1]
Mesotherapy originated in France with Michel Pistor; the French press coined the term in 1958, and the Académie Nationale de Médecine recognised it as a specialty in 1987.[1]

chain: Caffeine-containing injections placed in the skin of a target area
Intended to promote local fat breakdown
angle.text: Clinics offer it as a local fat and cellulite treatment, and proponents say it slims treated areas. Published support specific to caffeine has not been found.

paras: Mesotherapy delivers substances such as drugs, vitamins, hormones and plant extracts just beneath the skin. Practitioners use it for fat reduction, cellulite, skin rejuvenation and, in some clinics, pain conditions.[1] Caffeine is one of the ingredients associated with its fat-reduction use.

In the US, state medical boards rather than the FDA oversee practitioners who inject these mixtures; several South American countries have banned mesotherapy, and a 2011 French ban on fat removal was lifted after investigators tied problems to unhygienic conditions.[1] Plastic surgeon Rod Rohrich has said no data show it works, while the American Society for Dermatologic Surgery has said more study is needed.[1]

Reported problems in mesotherapy generally include skin abscesses and a mycobacterial infection in Australian clients; in a trial of deoxycholic acid, 81 percent of patients had mild, temporary reactions such as bruising, swelling and pain.[1]
No studies found. A small study of facial multivitamin mesotherapy in 10 patients, a different preparation, found no clinically relevant skin rejuvenation.[1]

timeline.event: The term mesotherapy is coined in the French press after Michel Pistor's clinical work.[1]
The French Académie Nationale de Médecine recognises mesotherapy as a specialty.[1]
